note: "they said" attributes to the envoys a statement the narrator makes, and "Their" is ambiguous.
replacement: Meanwhile the Syracusan envoys sent to Corinth and Lacedaemon were working their way along the coast, trying to persuade the Italiots to oppose the Athenians, whose proceedings threatened Italy as much as Syracuse. At Corinth the envoys made a speech asking for help on the ground of their common origin. The Corinthians voted at once to give it themselves, wholeheartedly, and then sent envoys along with them to Lacedaemon to help persuade her too to wage the war on the Athenians more openly at home, and to send succors to Sicily. When the Corinthian envoys reached Lacedaemon, they found Alcibiades there with his fellow refugees. He had crossed at once from Thurii in a trading vessel, first to Cyllene in Elis and then on to Lacedaemon, upon the Lacedaemonians’ own invitation and with a safe conduct obtained first, since he feared them because of his part in the affair of Mantinea. So in the assembly of the Lacedaemonians the Corinthians, the Syracusans and Alcibiades all pressed the same request, and persuaded them. But the ephors and the authorities resolved only to send envoys to Syracuse to stop it from surrendering to the Athenians. They showed no inclination to send any help. Alcibiades then came forward and stirred up and inflamed the Lacedaemonians with the following speech:

note: Source "may have been then unfairly angry" is stated flatly as "were unfairly angry".
replacement: “I must first speak to you about the prejudice against me, so that suspicion may not make you unwilling to hear me on public affairs. The connection with you as your proxeni had been renounced by my family’s ancestors out of some discontent. I personally tried to renew it by my good offices toward you, in particular at the time of the disaster at Pylos. Yet although I kept up this friendly attitude, you chose to make the peace with the Athenians through my enemies, and so to strengthen them and discredit me. You had no right, then, to complain when I turned to the Mantineans and Argives and took other opportunities to thwart and injure you. The time has now come for those of you who may have been unfairly angry with me in the bitterness of that moment to see the matter in its true light and take a different view. Others judged me unfavorably because I leaned toward the commons. They should not think their dislike any better founded. We have always been enemies of tyrants, and everyone who opposes arbitrary power is called commons. For that reason we continued as leaders of the multitude. Besides, democracy being the government of the city, in most things we had to conform to existing conditions. Still, we tried to be more moderate than the licentious temper of the times. Others, then as now, tried to lead the multitude astray — the very men who banished me. Our party was that of the whole people. Our creed was to do our part in preserving the form of government under which the city had enjoyed the utmost greatness and freedom, and which we had found in place. As for democracy, the men of sense among us knew what it was, and I perhaps as well as any, since I have more reason to complain of it. But there is nothing new to be said about a patent absurdity. And we did not think it safe to change it while you were pressing us with your hostility.

note: "What I felt it was when" is ungrammatical.
replacement: “Meanwhile I hope that none of you will think the worse of me because I, who until now passed for a lover of my country, am now actively joining its worst enemies to attack it. I hope too that you will not distrust my words as the product of an outlaw’s zeal. I am an outlaw through the iniquity of those who drove me out, but not, if you will be guided by me, from serving you. My worst enemies are not you, who only harmed your foes, but those who forced their friends to turn into enemies. When I am wronged I do not feel love of country. I felt it when I was secure in my rights as a citizen. In fact I do not think I am now attacking a country that is still mine. I am trying instead to win back one that is mine no longer. The true lover of his country is not the one who submits to losing it unjustly instead of attacking it. He is the one whose longing for it is so great that he will stop at nothing to recover it. For myself, Lacedaemonians, I beg you therefore to employ me without scruple in danger and hardship of every kind. Bear in mind the saying that everyone repeats: if I did you great harm as an enemy, I can also do you good service as a friend, since I know the plans of the Athenians and only guessed at yours. And I entreat you to believe, for your own part, that your most vital interests are now being weighed. Send the expeditions to Sicily and Attica without hesitation. With only a small part of your forces present, you will save important cities in that island and destroy the power of Athens, as it is now and as it may become. After that you will live in security and hold the supremacy over all Hellas, resting not on force but on consent and affection.”
